sectionTitle: How bonding and structure are related to the properties of substances

specStatements.text: The three states of matter are solid, liquid and gas. Melting and freezing take place at the melting point, boiling and condensing take place at the boiling point.

The three states of matter can be represented by a simple model. In this model, particles are represented by small solid spheres. Particle theory can help to explain melting, boiling, freezing and condensing.

The amount of energy needed to change state from solid to liquid and from liquid to gas depends on the strength of the forces between the particles of the substance. The nature of the particles involved depends on the type of bonding and the structure of the substance. The stronger the forces between the particles the higher the melting point and boiling point of the substance.
(HT only) Limitations of the simple model above include that in the model there are no forces, that all particles are represented as spheres and that the spheres are solid.
Students should be able to:
predict the states of substances at different temperatures given appropriate data
explain the different temperatures at which changes of state occur in terms of energy transfers and types of bonding
recognise that atoms themselves do not have the bulk properties of materials
(HT only) explain the limitations of the particle theory in relation to changes of state when particles are represented by solid inelastic spheres which have no forces between them.
In chemical equations, the three states of matter are shown as (s), (l) and (g), with (aq) for aqueous solutions.
Students should be able to include appropriate state symbols in chemical equations for the reactions in this specification.
Ionic compounds have regular structures (giant ionic lattices) in which there are strong electrostatic forces of attraction in all directions between oppositely charged ions.
These compounds have high melting points and high boiling points because of the large amounts of energy needed to break the many strong bonds.
When melted or dissolved in water, ionic compounds conduct electricity because the ions are free to move and so charge can flow.
Knowledge of the structures of specific ionic compounds other than sodium chloride is not required.
Substances that consist of small molecules are usually gases or liquids that have relatively low melting points and boiling points.
These substances have only weak forces between the molecules (intermolecular forces). It is these intermolecular forces that are overcome, not the covalent bonds, when the substance melts or boils.
The intermolecular forces increase with the size of the molecules, so larger molecules have higher melting and boiling points.
These substances do not conduct electricity because the molecules do not have an overall electric charge.
Students should be able to use the idea that intermolecular forces are weak compared with covalent bonds to explain the bulk properties of molecular substances.

Polymers have very large molecules. The atoms in the polymer molecules are linked to other atoms by strong covalent bonds. The intermolecular forces between polymer molecules are relatively strong and so these substances are solids at room temperature.
Students should be able to recognise polymers from diagrams showing their bonding and structure.

Substances that consist of giant covalent structures are solids with very high melting points. All of the atoms in these structures are linked to other atoms by strong covalent bonds. These bonds must be overcome to melt or boil these substances. Diamond and graphite (forms of carbon) and silicon dioxide (silica) are examples of giant covalent structures.
Students should be able to recognise giant covalent structures from diagrams showing their bonding and structure.
Metals have giant structures of atoms with strong metallic bonding. This means that most metals have high melting and boiling points.
In pure metals, atoms are arranged in layers, which allows metals to be bent and shaped. Pure metals are too soft for many uses and so are mixed with other metals to make alloys which are harder.

Metals are good conductors of electricity because the delocalised electrons in the metal carry electrical charge through the metal. Metals are good conductors of thermal energy because energy is transferred by the delocalised electrons.

scopeNotes.statement: Knowledge of the structures of specific ionic compounds other than sodium chloride is not required.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every question and example that asks students to describe or picture an ionic lattice uses sodium chloride. Other ionic compounds appear only where the property being tested follows from the general statements of 4.2.2.3 - that ionic compounds form giant lattices with strong electrostatic attraction in all directions, have high melting and boiling points, and conduct when molten or dissolved. Students are never asked to recall the arrangement, coordination number, unit cell or lattice type of magnesium oxide, calcium fluoride or any other named ionic compound, and no such structure is taught.

concepts.definition: Solid, liquid and gas. Every substance in this section is described as being in one of these three states at a stated temperature.
The temperature at which a substance changes between solid and liquid. Both melting and freezing take place at this one temperature; a substance does not have a separate freezing point.
The temperature at which a substance changes between liquid and gas. Both boiling and condensing take place at this one temperature.
Melting is the change from solid to liquid; freezing is the change from liquid to solid. Both take place at the melting point.
Boiling is the change from liquid to gas; condensing is the change from gas to liquid. Both take place at the boiling point.

concepts.term: The simple model of the states of matter
concepts.definition: A model in which the particles of a substance are represented by small solid spheres. Particle theory used with this model helps to explain melting, boiling, freezing and condensing.
The attractions holding the particles of a substance together. The stronger these forces, the higher the melting point and boiling point of the substance.

The energy needed to go from solid to liquid, or from liquid to gas, depends on the strength of the forces between the particles. What those particles are depends on the type of bonding and the structure of the substance.

concepts.term: Limitations of the simple model (HT only)
concepts.definition: In the simple model there are no forces between the particles, all particles are represented as spheres, and the spheres are solid. Because the model contains no forces, it cannot explain why energy must be supplied to change state, or why different substances change state at different temperatures.

Properties such as melting point, conductivity and being able to be bent and shaped, which belong to a large amount of a substance and not to its individual atoms. A single atom does not have the bulk properties of the material it is part of.
The labels written after each formula in a chemical equation to show the state of that substance: (s) for solid, (l) for liquid and (g) for gas, with (aq) for aqueous solutions.
A substance dissolved in water. It is labelled (aq) in an equation, not (l); (l) is used only for a pure liquid such as water itself.
The regular structure of an ionic compound, in which very many oppositely charged ions are arranged in a repeating pattern. Sodium chloride is the example used in this specification.

concepts.term: Electrostatic forces of attraction in an ionic lattice
concepts.definition: The strong attractions between oppositely charged ions in a giant ionic lattice. They act in all directions, not just between one pair of ions.

concepts.term: Melting and boiling points of ionic compounds
concepts.definition: Ionic compounds have high melting points and high boiling points, because large amounts of energy are needed to break the many strong bonds in the lattice.
When melted or dissolved in water, ionic compounds conduct electricity, because the ions are then free to move and so charge can flow. In the solid the ions are held in fixed positions.
Substances that consist of small molecules are usually gases or liquids with relatively low melting points and boiling points. Water, methane, chlorine and ammonia are examples.
The weak forces acting between whole molecules. It is these forces, and not the covalent bonds, that are overcome when a molecular substance melts or boils.

concepts.term: Covalent bond compared with intermolecular force
concepts.definition: A covalent bond joins atoms inside a molecule and is strong. The forces between separate molecules are weak by comparison. This difference explains the bulk properties of molecular substances.

concepts.term: Why molecular substances do not conduct
concepts.definition: Substances made of molecules do not conduct electricity because the molecules do not have an overall electric charge, so there is nothing charged that can move and carry current.
The intermolecular forces increase with the size of the molecules, so larger molecules have higher melting and boiling points than smaller ones.
A substance whose molecules are very large. In a diagram a polymer appears as long chains of repeating units. Polymers are solids at room temperature.

The atoms within a polymer molecule are linked to other atoms by strong covalent bonds. The intermolecular forces between the polymer molecules are relatively strong, which is why polymers are solids at room temperature.

A structure in which all of the atoms are linked to other atoms by strong covalent bonds. These substances are solids with very high melting points, because those bonds must be overcome to melt or boil them.
Diamond and graphite, which are forms of carbon, and silicon dioxide, also called silica.

concepts.term: Metallic bonding in a giant structure
concepts.definition: Metals have giant structures of atoms held together by strong metallic bonding, which is why most metals have high melting and boiling points.

concepts.term: Layers of atoms in a pure metal
concepts.definition: In pure metals the atoms are arranged in layers. The layers can slide over each other, which allows metals to be bent and shaped.
A metal mixed with other metals. Pure metals are too soft for many uses, so they are made into alloys, which are harder because atoms of different sizes distort the layers.
The electrons in a metal that are not held to one atom. They carry electrical charge through the metal, which is why metals are good conductors of electricity.
Metals are good conductors of thermal energy because energy is transferred by the delocalised electrons moving through the structure.

misconceptions.question: Does a substance have a freezing point that is different from its melting point?
misconceptions.correct: No. Melting and freezing both take place at the melting point, and boiling and condensing both take place at the boiling point.
misconceptions.misconception: Every change of state has its own temperature, so a substance has a melting point, a freezing point, a boiling point and a condensing point - four different numbers.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday language gives each change its own name, so students assume each name must come with its own temperature. Data books only ever quote two values, but students rarely notice that the missing two are not missing at all.
misconceptions.correction: There are only two temperatures. At the melting point the substance can go either way, solid to liquid or liquid to solid; at the boiling point it can go liquid to gas or gas to liquid. Ice melts at 0 degrees C and water freezes at 0 degrees C - the same temperature, travelled in opposite directions.

misconceptions.question: A gas turns into a liquid. Is that condensing or freezing, and where does it happen?
misconceptions.correct: It is condensing, and it takes place at the boiling point.
misconceptions.misconception: Condensing and freezing are the same thing, because both happen when something is cooled down.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both changes are produced by cooling and both are seen on cold surfaces - breath on a window, ice on a freezer wall - so students treat them as one process rather than two changes between different pairs of states.
misconceptions.correction: Name the states at each end. Gas to liquid is condensing, at the boiling point. Liquid to solid is freezing, at the melting point. Cooling steam gives water at 100 degrees C; cooling that water further gives ice at 0 degrees C.

misconceptions.question: When a substance is heated, do the particles themselves get bigger?
misconceptions.correct: No. The particles stay the same; they gain energy, move more and end up further apart.
misconceptions.misconception: Heating makes each particle swell up, and that is why a substance expands and eventually melts.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students transfer what they can see - the whole sample expanding - onto the individual particles, because the model draws particles as objects that look as though they could stretch.
misconceptions.correction: In the model the spheres never change. What changes is how much energy they have, how fast they move and how far apart they sit. Expansion is extra spacing between particles, not bigger particles.

misconceptions.question: In the simple model of the states of matter, what is a particle drawn as?
misconceptions.correct: A small solid sphere, with no internal detail shown.
misconceptions.misconception: The particles in the model are drawn as atoms with a nucleus and electron shells, and the model's weakness is that it forgets to show the electrons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students have just met atomic structure in 4.1, so they carry that picture over and judge the states-of-matter model by whether it shows subatomic particles.
misconceptions.correction: The simple model deliberately shows nothing inside a particle: it is a small solid sphere. Its real limitations are that it contains no forces, that everything is drawn as a sphere, and that the spheres are solid.

misconceptions.question: If the forces between particles are stronger, what happens to the melting point?
misconceptions.correct: It is higher, because more energy is needed to separate the particles.
misconceptions.misconception: Stronger forces mean the particles are held so tightly that they break apart more easily, so the melting point is lower.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students confuse being tightly held with being under strain, and some reason that strong forces mean a small, tight structure and therefore less to overcome.
misconceptions.correction: Melting means overcoming the forces. The stronger they are, the more energy is needed, so the higher the temperature must be. Stronger forces always mean a higher melting point and a higher boiling point.

misconceptions.question: Does a substance melt at a high temperature because its particles are heavy?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is the strength of the forces between the particles that decides the melting point.
misconceptions.misconception: Heavy particles are hard to move, so the heavier the particles the higher the melting point.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday experience says heavy things are hard to shift, and the periodic table gives students a mass figure for every element, so mass is the number nearest to hand.
misconceptions.correction: The specification is explicit: the energy needed to change state depends on the strength of the forces between the particles. Sodium chloride melts near 800 degrees C and chlorine boils at -34 degrees C, even though a chlorine molecule is heavier than a sodium ion. Forces, not mass, set the temperature.

misconceptions.question: A substance is at a temperature between its melting point and its boiling point. What state is it in?
misconceptions.correct: It is a liquid, throughout that whole range of temperature.
misconceptions.misconception: Between the two temperatures the substance is only partly melted, so it is a mixture of solid and liquid.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students picture melting as something that happens gradually over the whole range rather than at one temperature, so 'in between' feels like 'in between states'.
misconceptions.correction: Melting is complete at the melting point. Above it and below the boiling point the substance is entirely liquid. Water is liquid at 1 degree C and at 99 degrees C alike.

misconceptions.question: A substance boils at 59 degrees C. At 25 degrees C, must it be a solid because 25 is below 59?
misconceptions.correct: No. You must check the melting point too. At 25 degrees C it is above the melting point, so it is a liquid.
misconceptions.misconception: If the temperature is below the boiling point the substance has not turned into anything yet, so it is still a solid.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students compare the temperature with one value instead of two, and the boiling point is usually the larger, more eye-catching number in the table.
misconceptions.correction: Always use both values. Below the melting point it is solid; between the melting point and boiling point it is liquid; above the boiling point it is a gas. Bromine, melting point -7 degrees C and boiling point 59 degrees C, is a liquid at 25 degrees C.

misconceptions.question: A substance melts at -219 degrees C. At -200 degrees C, is it a gas because it is above the melting point?
misconceptions.correct: No. Above the melting point it has become a liquid; it is a gas only above the boiling point.
misconceptions.misconception: Once the temperature passes the melting point the substance has changed completely, so it must be a gas.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students treat 'melting point passed' as 'fully changed', skipping the liquid state entirely, especially when both values are negative and hard to order.
misconceptions.correction: Place the temperature on a number line between the two values. Oxygen melts at -219 degrees C and boils at -183 degrees C, so at -200 degrees C it lies between them and is a liquid.

misconceptions.question: Is a substance at -200 degrees C bound to be a solid?
misconceptions.correct: No. Whether it is solid depends on its own melting point, not on the temperature sounding cold.
misconceptions.misconception: Very low temperatures always mean a solid, because everything freezes when it gets cold enough.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students judge by everyday feel rather than by the data given, and -200 degrees C sounds far colder than anything they can imagine staying liquid.
misconceptions.correction: Use the data. Oxygen is still liquid at -200 degrees C because its melting point is -219 degrees C. A temperature is only 'cold' relative to a particular substance's melting and boiling points.

misconceptions.question: Copper wire can be bent. Can a single copper atom be bent and shaped?
misconceptions.correct: No. Being able to be bent and shaped is a bulk property; a single atom does not have it.
misconceptions.misconception: One atom of copper is just a very tiny piece of copper, so it behaves like copper in every way.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students reason that a substance is made of its atoms, so each atom must be a miniature sample carrying all the same properties.
misconceptions.correction: Bending depends on layers of atoms sliding over one another, which needs many atoms arranged in a structure. One atom has no layers and nothing to slide, so the property simply does not exist at that scale.

misconceptions.question: Sodium chloride is dissolved in water. Which state symbol is used?
misconceptions.correct: (aq), which stands for an aqueous solution.
misconceptions.misconception: A solution is a liquid, so it should be labelled (l).
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students classify by what they see in the beaker rather than by the meaning of the symbols, and a solution certainly looks and pours like a liquid.
misconceptions.correction: (l) is kept for a pure substance that is liquid on its own, such as water in H2O(l) or molten lead. Anything dissolved in water is (aq): NaCl(aq), HCl(aq), NaOH(aq).

misconceptions.question: Zinc chloride forms in solution during a reaction. Is it written ZnCl2(s)?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is written ZnCl2(aq), because it is dissolved in the water.
misconceptions.misconception: Zinc chloride is a solid substance, so it keeps the symbol (s) wherever it appears in the equation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students attach the state symbol to the substance as they know it from a bottle on the shelf, instead of to the substance as it is in that particular reaction mixture.
misconceptions.correction: The state symbol describes the substance during the reaction. In Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) → ZnCl2(aq) + H2(g), the zinc chloride never appears as a solid: it forms dissolved in the acid.

misconceptions.question: In sodium chloride, is each sodium ion attracted to just one chloride ion?
misconceptions.correct: No. There are strong electrostatic forces of attraction in all directions between oppositely charged ions.
misconceptions.misconception: The sodium atom gave its electron to one particular chlorine atom, so those two ions are bonded to each other as a pair.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The dot and cross diagram used to show electron transfer draws exactly one sodium and one chlorine, so students carry that pairing over into the structure of the solid.
misconceptions.correction: Electron transfer explains where the charges come from; it does not fix which ions attract. Once formed, every ion attracts all the oppositely charged ions around it in all directions, which is what makes it a giant lattice.

misconceptions.question: Is solid sodium chloride made of NaCl molecules?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is a giant ionic lattice of sodium ions and chloride ions.
misconceptions.misconception: The formula NaCl means one particle containing one sodium and one chlorine, so the solid is a heap of NaCl molecules.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students read every formula the way they read H2O or CO2, as the recipe for a single molecule, rather than as the ratio of ions in a lattice.
misconceptions.correction: For an ionic compound the formula gives the simplest ratio of ions, here one Na+ to one Cl-. The solid contains enormous numbers of both, held in a repeating three-dimensional pattern, with no molecules at all.

misconceptions.question: Does solid sodium chloride contain ions?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The ions are there in the solid, but they are held in fixed positions and cannot move.
misconceptions.misconception: The ions are only made when the compound is melted or dissolved, which is why the solid does not conduct.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students link 'conducts' with 'has ions', so if the solid does not conduct they conclude the ions cannot be present yet.
misconceptions.correction: The difference is movement, not existence. The lattice is built from ions all along; melting or dissolving frees them to move, and only then can charge flow.

misconceptions.question: What carries the charge when molten sodium chloride conducts electricity?
misconceptions.correct: The ions, which are free to move once the lattice has been broken up.
misconceptions.misconception: Melting releases electrons, and it is those electrons that carry the current, as in a metal.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Every other conductor students have met - copper wire, a filament - conducts by electrons, so electrons become the default explanation for any conduction.
misconceptions.correction: Ionic compounds have no delocalised electrons. In molten or dissolved ionic compounds the moving charged particles are the ions themselves, and it is their movement that lets charge flow.

misconceptions.question: Sugar is dissolved in water. Will the solution conduct electricity?
misconceptions.correct: No. Sugar is molecular, so the solution contains no ions and no charge can flow.
misconceptions.misconception: Anything that has been dissolved or melted will conduct, because its particles are now free to move.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember the rule 'melted or dissolved conducts' as a fact about liquids in general, dropping the part that says it applies to ionic compounds because their particles are charged.
misconceptions.correction: Free movement is only half the requirement; the moving particles must also be charged. Sugar molecules move freely in solution but carry no overall charge, so nothing conducts.

misconceptions.question: Are all substances made of small molecules gases?
misconceptions.correct: No. They are usually gases or liquids, and some are solids with low melting points.
misconceptions.misconception: Small molecules means small forces means gas, so every simple molecular substance must be a gas at room temperature.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The examples met first - oxygen, chlorine, methane, ammonia - are all gases, so students turn a common case into a rule and skip over the word 'usually'.
misconceptions.correction: Read the word 'usually'. Water is a liquid at room temperature and iodine is a solid, yet both consist of small molecules. What the statement guarantees is relatively low melting and boiling points, not one particular state.

misconceptions.question: When water boils, are the O-H covalent bonds broken?
misconceptions.correct: No. Only the weak intermolecular forces between the molecules are overcome.
misconceptions.misconception: Boiling breaks the substance up, so it must be breaking the bonds inside the molecules.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students see boiling as a dramatic change and assume it costs the largest bond-breaking energy available; the phrase 'breaking bonds' also gets used loosely for any separation.
misconceptions.correction: Steam is still made of H2O molecules - the covalent bonds survive. Boiling only pulls whole molecules apart from each other, which is why it happens at 100 degrees C, while splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen needs far more energy.

misconceptions.question: Are the particles in bromine or in silicon dioxide held together by ionic attraction?
misconceptions.correct: No. Both substances contain non-metal atoms joined by covalent bonds, not oppositely charged ions.
misconceptions.misconception: Any strong attraction holding a substance together must be the attraction between positive and negative ions.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Ionic bonding is taught first and is described as strong and electrostatic, so students reach for it whenever they need to explain a strong attraction, even between two non-metals.
misconceptions.correction: Check the elements. Non-metal with non-metal means covalent. Br2 is two bromine atoms sharing a pair of electrons; silicon dioxide is a giant network of covalent bonds. No ions are formed in either.

misconceptions.question: Two molecular substances differ in molecular size. Which has the higher boiling point?
misconceptions.correct: The one with the larger molecules, because the intermolecular forces increase with molecular size.
misconceptions.misconception: Bigger molecules are clumsier and further apart, so the forces between them are weaker and they boil at a lower temperature.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students picture large molecules as taking up more room and therefore being more spread out, and they have no reason yet to link size with strength of attraction.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states it directly: intermolecular forces increase with the size of the molecules, so larger molecules have higher melting and boiling points. The size of the molecule, not the strength of its covalent bonds, is what changes.

misconceptions.question: Why does a molecular substance such as methane not conduct electricity?
misconceptions.correct: Because its molecules do not have an overall electric charge.
misconceptions.misconception: It does not conduct because its electrons are all locked into covalent bonds, so there are no free electrons.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students carry the metal explanation across and look for missing free electrons, which sounds convincing and is not entirely wrong - but it is not the reason the specification gives.
misconceptions.correction: Give the reason as the specification does: the molecules have no overall charge, so there is no charged particle that can move through the substance and carry current.

misconceptions.question: Are the chains in a polymer joined to each other by covalent bonds?
misconceptions.correct: No. Covalent bonds join the atoms within a chain; the chains are held to each other by intermolecular forces.
misconceptions.misconception: Everything in a polymer is covalently bonded, so the chains must be bonded to each other as well.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students are told polymers contain strong covalent bonds and apply it to the whole structure, without separating what happens along a chain from what happens between chains.
misconceptions.correction: Distinguish the two. Along the chain: strong covalent bonds. Between chains: intermolecular forces, which are relatively strong for polymers because the molecules are very large - strong enough to make polymers solid at room temperature, but still not covalent bonds.

misconceptions.question: Why is a polymer a solid at room temperature?
misconceptions.correct: Because the intermolecular forces between its very large molecules are relatively strong.
misconceptions.misconception: It is a solid because the covalent bonds inside the polymer molecules are strong.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students know covalent bonds are strong and reach for the strongest thing in the structure, without asking which forces are actually overcome when a substance melts.
misconceptions.correction: Melting a molecular substance overcomes the forces between molecules, so those are the forces that decide the state. Poly(ethene) and hexane both contain strong covalent bonds, yet hexane is a liquid: the difference is molecular size and therefore intermolecular force.

misconceptions.question: A diagram shows long chains of repeating units. Is that a giant covalent structure?
misconceptions.correct: No. Long separate chains show a polymer; a giant covalent structure is a network in which every atom is bonded into one continuous structure.
misconceptions.misconception: Both have lots of atoms joined by covalent bonds, so a polymer diagram and a giant covalent diagram show the same kind of structure.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Polymers are sometimes called macromolecules, and both structures look large and covalently bonded on the page, so students group them together.
misconceptions.correction: Look for gaps between chains. A polymer is many separate very large molecules lying alongside each other. In diamond or silicon dioxide there are no separate molecules at all - every atom is linked on to the next through the whole structure.

misconceptions.question: Silicon dioxide and carbon dioxide have similar formulae. Do they have similar structures?
misconceptions.correct: No. Carbon dioxide consists of small molecules; silicon dioxide is a giant covalent structure.
misconceptions.misconception: SiO2 is a small molecule like CO2, so silica should be a gas or at least melt easily.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The formulae look alike and silicon sits directly below carbon, so students expect matching structures and properties.
misconceptions.correction: In silicon dioxide every atom is joined on to others by strong covalent bonds through the whole structure, so it is a solid with a very high melting point. The formula gives only the ratio of atoms, not the size of the structure.

misconceptions.question: A diagram shows a regular three-dimensional network of particles. Must it be ionic?
misconceptions.correct: No. Giant covalent structures and metals are also regular three-dimensional structures.
misconceptions.misconception: Any repeating lattice drawn in three dimensions is an ionic lattice, because that is what lattices are.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word lattice is introduced with ionic bonding, so students treat the visual pattern as the signature of ionic structure rather than of regularity in general.
misconceptions.correction: Read what the particles are. Alternating positive and negative ions means ionic. Identical atoms joined by covalent bonds throughout means giant covalent. Identical atoms in close-packed layers means a metal.

misconceptions.question: Is a piece of iron made of iron molecules?
misconceptions.correct: No. Metals have giant structures of atoms held together by strong metallic bonding.
misconceptions.misconception: Solids are made of molecules held together, so a metal is made of metal molecules.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Molecule becomes a general word for 'the particle a substance is made of', so students apply it to every substance including metals.
misconceptions.correction: A metal has no molecules. It is one giant structure of atoms, which is why metallic bonding must be overcome throughout the whole structure and why most metals have high melting and boiling points.

misconceptions.question: Why can a pure metal be bent without snapping?
misconceptions.correct: Because its atoms are arranged in layers that can slide over each other.
misconceptions.misconception: Bending a metal breaks the metallic bonds, which is why it gives way rather than shattering.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate any change of shape with something breaking, and bonds are the only thing available to break in their picture of the structure.
misconceptions.correction: The layers slide, and the metallic bonding is maintained as they do so. If the bonding were broken the metal would simply come apart; instead it holds together in its new shape.

misconceptions.question: Which is harder, a pure metal or an alloy of it?
misconceptions.correct: The alloy. Pure metals are too soft for many uses, so they are mixed with other metals to make alloys, which are harder.
misconceptions.misconception: Pure means better and stronger, so a pure metal must be harder than a mixture.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday use 'pure' signals high quality, and students meet purity elsewhere in chemistry as something to aim for, so softness sounds like a fault of a mixture.
misconceptions.correction: Purity and hardness are unrelated. In a pure metal the identical atoms lie in even layers that slide easily. An alloy contains atoms of different sizes, which distort the layers so they cannot slide as easily, making the alloy harder.

misconceptions.question: What moves through a metal when it conducts electricity?
misconceptions.correct: The delocalised electrons, which carry electrical charge through the metal.
misconceptions.misconception: The metal atoms or ions themselves travel through the metal carrying the charge.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students have just learnt that in molten ionic compounds it is the ions that move, so they transfer that explanation to metals, which also contain positive ions.
misconceptions.correction: In a metal the positive ions stay in their fixed positions in the giant structure; only the delocalised electrons move. That is also how metals conduct thermal energy - energy is transferred by those same electrons.

misconceptions.question: Why do metals conduct thermal energy so well?
misconceptions.correct: Because energy is transferred by the delocalised electrons.
misconceptions.misconception: Metals conduct heat because they are dense and their particles are packed tightly together.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Metals feel cold and heavy, and students know that packed particles pass vibrations on well, so density becomes the explanation for a property they have felt directly.
misconceptions.correction: Tight packing alone is not enough - diamond and sodium chloride are packed just as tightly. What metals have that those do not is delocalised electrons, and it is those electrons that transfer the energy.

misconceptions.question: Copper conducts electricity. Does a single copper atom conduct electricity?
misconceptions.correct: No. Conduction is a bulk property that depends on delocalised electrons moving through a giant structure.
misconceptions.misconception: Conducting is a property of the element copper, so every copper atom conducts and shines on its own.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Properties are listed against element names in tables, so students attach them to the element as a label rather than to the arrangement of many atoms.
misconceptions.correction: Conduction needs electrons travelling from one place to another through a structure of many atoms. A lone atom offers nowhere for charge to travel to, so the property does not exist at that scale.

misconceptions.question: Does the symbol (aq) mean that water is mixed in with the substance?
misconceptions.correct: It means the substance is dissolved in water, forming an aqueous solution.
misconceptions.misconception: (aq) shows that the substance is damp or has water trapped in its crystals.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students recognise that (aq) has something to do with water but not exactly what, so they settle on the loosest version - water being present somewhere.
misconceptions.correction: (aq) is short for aqueous, and it means dissolved in water so that the particles are separated and free to move. A damp solid is still written (s).

misconceptions.question: Which are stronger, covalent bonds or the forces between molecules?
misconceptions.correct: Covalent bonds are strong; the intermolecular forces between molecules are weak by comparison.
misconceptions.misconception: The forces holding a substance together must be the strongest thing in it, so the forces between molecules are stronger than the covalent bonds.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students reason from the outcome: a substance holds together as a solid or liquid, so whatever holds it together must be the strongest force present.
misconceptions.correction: Compare the energies through observation. Water boils at 100 degrees C, which only separates whole molecules, but splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen needs far more energy because it breaks covalent bonds. Weak forces between, strong bonds within.

misconceptions.question: Does mixing metals together make the material melt more easily and become weaker?
misconceptions.correct: Mixing metals makes alloys, which are harder than the pure metals they are made from.
misconceptions.misconception: Adding another metal contaminates the structure and weakens it, so an alloy is softer than the pure metal.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Impurity sounds like damage, and students know that impurities lower the melting point of a substance, so they extend that to every property.
misconceptions.correction: The specification is explicit: pure metals are too soft for many uses and so are mixed with other metals to make alloys which are harder. Atoms of a different size disrupt the even layers, so the layers cannot slide over each other so easily.

misconceptions.question: How does charge travel along a copper wire?
misconceptions.correct: Delocalised electrons move through the whole metal, carrying electrical charge.
misconceptions.misconception: Each atom passes an electron on to the next atom in a chain, like a relay.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The hand-to-hand image is intuitive and matches diagrams of electrons drawn sitting on individual atoms, which is exactly what delocalisation removes.
misconceptions.correction: The electrons are not attached to any particular atom to begin with - they are delocalised throughout the giant structure and are free to move through it, so charge flows without any handing over.

mcqs.stem: At which temperature does a liquid change into a solid?

options.text: Its freezing point, a lower temperature than melting
options.rationale: Students who expect every named change to have its own temperature invent a separate freezing point below the melting point.

options.text: Its boiling point, where condensing also takes place
options.rationale: Freezing and condensing are treated as the same cooling process, so the boiling point is chosen for both.

options.text: Its melting point, the same temperature as melting
options.rationale: Melting and freezing both take place at the melting point, as the specification states.

options.text: Any temperature that is below room temperature
options.rationale: Freezing is judged by whether the surroundings feel cold rather than against the substance's own melting point.

mcqs.stem: A gas is cooled until it turns into a liquid. What is this change called, and at what temperature does it happen?

options.text: Freezing, which happens at the boiling point
options.rationale: The change is caused by cooling, so it gets labelled freezing even though the states involved are gas and liquid.

options.text: Condensing, which happens at the boiling point
options.rationale: Gas to liquid is condensing, and boiling and condensing both take place at the boiling point.

options.text: Condensing, which happens at the melting point
options.rationale: The change is named correctly but attached to the wrong one of the two temperatures.

options.text: Evaporating, which happens at the melting point
options.rationale: Evaporating is confused with condensing because both involve a liquid and a gas, without checking the direction.

mcqs.stem: In the simple model of the three states of matter, how are the particles represented?

options.text: As spheres that expand when the substance is heated
options.rationale: Students who think heating makes particles swell expect the model to show the spheres growing.

options.text: As small solid spheres, all drawn in the same way
options.rationale: The specification states that in this model particles are represented by small solid spheres.

options.text: As small spheres joined by springs that show forces
options.rationale: Bonding models seen elsewhere include springs or sticks, so students import them into this model.

options.text: As atoms drawn with the nucleus and electron shells
options.rationale: Atomic structure from 4.1 is carried over, although this model deliberately shows no internal detail.

mcqs.stem: Substance X has stronger forces between its particles than substance Y. What does this tell you?

options.text: X has a lower melting point and boiling point than Y
options.rationale: Strong forces are read as a strained, tightly held structure that gives way more easily.

options.text: X has a higher melting point and boiling point than Y
options.rationale: The stronger the forces between particles, the higher the melting point and boiling point.

options.text: X melts at a higher temperature but boils at a lower one
options.rationale: The two temperatures are treated as unconnected values that need not respond to the forces in the same way.

options.text: X and Y melt at exactly the same temperature as one another
options.rationale: Chosen by students who believe the melting point is set by the mass of the particles rather than by the forces.

mcqs.stem: What decides the nature of the particles that are held together in a substance?

options.text: The temperature at which the substance is being kept
options.rationale: Students who think heating changes the particles themselves expect temperature to decide what the particles are.

options.text: The number of particles present in the sample being used
options.rationale: Amount of substance is confused with the kind of particle, since both are described by counting.

options.text: The type of bonding and the structure of the substance
options.rationale: The specification states that the nature of the particles involved depends on the type of bonding and the structure.

options.text: How heavy each individual particle in the substance is
options.rationale: Mass is the most familiar number attached to a particle, so it is chosen as the deciding factor.

mcqs.stem: Higher tier. Which of these is a limitation of the simple model of the states of matter?

options.text: In the model the particles are shown vibrating too fast
options.rationale: Sounds like a criticism of the model's realism, but speed of vibration is not one of the stated limitations.

options.text: In the model the electrons in each particle are left out
options.rationale: Students judge the model against atomic structure, expecting it to show subatomic detail it never claims to show.

options.text: In the model there are no forces between the particles
options.rationale: The specification lists this first among the limitations of the simple model.

options.text: In the model each particle expands as it is being heated
options.rationale: Chosen by students who wrongly believe particles themselves grow on heating, so they read this as a flaw.

mcqs.stem: Bromine melts at -7 degrees C and boils at 59 degrees C. Which statement about bromine at 25 degrees C is correct?

options.text: It is solid, as 25 has not yet reached 59
options.rationale: The temperature is compared only with the boiling point, so the melting point is never checked.

options.text: It is liquid, as 25 is above -7 but below 59
options.rationale: A temperature between the melting point and the boiling point means the substance is entirely liquid.

options.text: It is a gas, as 25 is already well above -7
options.rationale: Passing the melting point is read as the substance having changed all the way to a gas.

options.text: It is part solid, part liquid, as 25 is between
options.rationale: Melting is pictured as happening gradually across the whole range rather than at one temperature.

mcqs.stem: Oxygen melts at -219 degrees C and boils at -183 degrees C. What is the state of oxygen at -200 degrees C?

options.text: Liquid, since -200 lies between the two values given
options.rationale: -200 is above the melting point of -219 and below the boiling point of -183, so oxygen is liquid.

options.text: Solid, since -200 is an extremely low temperature
options.rationale: The temperature is judged as 'very cold' by everyday feel instead of against the data given.

options.text: Gas, since -200 is higher than the melting point
options.rationale: Being above the melting point is taken to mean the substance has become a gas.

options.text: Solid, since -200 is below the boiling point given
options.rationale: Only the boiling point is used, and negative values make the ordering harder to check.

mcqs.stem: Sodium chloride must be heated to about 800 degrees C to melt it, but ice melts at 0 degrees C. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: Its particles are much heavier than water molecules are
options.rationale: Mass is used in place of force strength as the explanation for a high melting point.

options.text: Water molecules are smaller, so they melt more easily
options.rationale: Size of the particle is treated as the deciding factor rather than the forces between particles.

options.text: Its ions are held by much stronger forces of attraction
options.rationale: More energy is needed because the electrostatic attraction between ions is far stronger than the forces between water molecules.

options.text: Water has covalent bonds, which are weaker than ionic
options.rationale: Melting ice is assumed to break the covalent bonds inside water molecules, so bond strengths get compared.

mcqs.stem: Chlorine boils at -34 degrees C while sodium chloride boils at about 1400 degrees C. Which explanation of this difference is correct?

options.text: Weak covalent bonds in Cl2, strong ionic bonds in NaCl
options.rationale: Boiling chlorine is assumed to break its covalent bond, so the comparison is made between the wrong two things.

options.text: Weak forces between Cl2 molecules, strong forces between ions
options.rationale: Boiling chlorine only overcomes weak intermolecular forces; boiling sodium chloride must overcome strong electrostatic attraction between ions.

options.text: Cl2 molecules are far lighter, so they escape more easily
options.rationale: Mass replaces force strength, and chlorine gas being light is easy to picture.

options.text: Chlorine is already a gas, so no forces need overcoming
options.rationale: The state at room temperature is confused with the explanation for that state.

mcqs.stem: A copper wire conducts electricity and can be bent into shape. Which statement about a single copper atom is correct?

options.text: It does not have these bulk properties on its own
options.rationale: The specification requires students to recognise that atoms themselves do not have the bulk properties of materials.

options.text: It can be bent and shaped, as a piece of copper can
options.rationale: A single atom is treated as a miniature sample of copper carrying all the same properties.

options.text: It conducts electricity, because copper is a conductor
options.rationale: Conduction is attached to the element as a label rather than to a structure of many atoms.

options.text: It gains both properties as soon as it is warmed up
options.rationale: Heating is assumed to switch on properties, which confuses change of state with change of property.

mcqs.stem: Higher tier. A student says the simple particle model explains why energy must be supplied to boil water. Why is this wrong?

options.text: The model draws each particle expanding as it is heated
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think the model shows particles growing, which it does not.

options.text: The model does not show the electrons in each particle
options.rationale: A real omission from the drawing, but not one that has anything to do with the energy of boiling.

options.text: The model shows liquids and gases with the same spacing
options.rationale: Sounds like a plausible criticism, but the model does show gases with the particles further apart.

options.text: The model has no forces between particles to overcome
options.rationale: Because the model contains no forces, it offers nothing that the supplied energy could be used to overcome.

mcqs.stem: What does the state symbol (aq) mean in a chemical equation?

options.text: Dissolved in water, forming an aqueous solution
options.rationale: (aq) is used for aqueous solutions, that is substances dissolved in water.

options.text: A liquid element or compound at room temperature
options.rationale: Solutions look and pour like liquids, so (aq) is read as another way of saying liquid.

options.text: A damp solid with water trapped in its crystals
options.rationale: Students know (aq) involves water but settle on water simply being present rather than dissolving.

options.text: Any solution at all, whichever solvent was used
options.rationale: The 'aqueous' part is dropped, so the symbol is over-generalised to all solvents.

mcqs.stem: Zinc is added to dilute hydrochloric acid. Which equation has the state symbols written correctly?

options.text: Zn(s) + 2HCl(l) → ZnCl2(l) + H2(g)
options.rationale: The acid and the solution formed are labelled (l) because they are liquids in the beaker.

options.text: Zn(aq) + 2HCl(aq) → ZnCl2(s) + H2(g)
options.rationale: Zinc chloride keeps the label (s) because students know it as a solid from the bottle.

options.text: Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) → ZnCl2(aq) + H2(aq)
options.rationale: The hydrogen is labelled (aq) because it is produced in a solution, rather than (g) as a gas escaping.

options.text: Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) → ZnCl2(aq) + H2(g)
options.rationale: The zinc is a solid, the acid and the salt formed are dissolved in water, and hydrogen is released as a gas.

mcqs.stem: Dilute hydrochloric acid is neutralised by sodium hydroxide solution. Which equation has the state symbols written correctly?

options.text: HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(s) + H2O(l)
options.rationale: Sodium chloride is labelled (s) because it is familiar as a solid, although here it remains dissolved.

options.text: HCl(aq) + NaOH(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H2O(l)
options.rationale: Both reactants are in solution, the salt formed stays dissolved, and the water produced is a pure liquid.

options.text: HCl(l) + NaOH(l) → NaCl(aq) + H2O(aq)
options.rationale: The two solutions are labelled (l) because they are liquids, and water is labelled (aq) because it is watery.

options.text: HCl(aq) + NaOH(s) → NaCl(aq) + H2O(g)
options.rationale: The alkali is treated as a solid and the water as steam, because neutralisation is known to be exothermic.

mcqs.stem: Which statement describes the structure of an ionic compound such as sodium chloride?

options.text: A regular lattice with strong attraction in all directions
options.rationale: Ionic compounds have giant ionic lattices with strong electrostatic forces of attraction in all directions between oppositely charged ions.

options.text: Pairs of ions each joined by one strong bond in the pair
options.rationale: The dot and cross diagram shows one sodium and one chlorine, so students keep them paired in the solid.

options.text: A regular lattice of atoms held by shared electron pairs
options.rationale: Ionic and covalent bonding are blended, keeping the lattice but replacing the ions with shared electrons.

options.text: Molecules of NaCl packed closely in a regular pattern
options.rationale: The formula NaCl is read as the recipe for a molecule, as H2O or CO2 would be.

mcqs.stem: Why do ionic compounds have high melting points and high boiling points?

options.text: The ions themselves are heavy and so are hard to move
options.rationale: Mass is used in place of force strength as the explanation of a high melting point.

options.text: Large amounts of energy break the many strong bonds
options.rationale: This is the specification's own reason: large amounts of energy are needed to break the many strong bonds.

options.text: The covalent bonds inside the lattice are very strong
options.rationale: Bond types are mixed up: 'strong bonds' is remembered, but labelled covalent instead of ionic.

options.text: Each ion is bonded to just one oppositely charged ion
options.rationale: The lattice is pictured as pairs, which would not explain why so much energy is needed.

mcqs.stem: Solid sodium chloride does not conduct electricity, but molten sodium chloride does. Why?

options.text: Melting releases electrons that then move through it
options.rationale: Conduction by electrons is the familiar case from metals, so it is applied here too.

options.text: Melting turns the ions into atoms that can carry charge
options.rationale: Melting is assumed to change the particles chemically rather than simply free them to move.

options.text: In the liquid the ions are free to move and carry charge
options.rationale: Melting frees the ions from their fixed positions, so charge can flow.

options.text: The solid contains no ions until it is melted or dissolved
options.rationale: Not conducting is taken to mean no ions are present, rather than ions that cannot move.

mcqs.stem: Which of these will conduct electricity?

options.text: Solid sodium chloride at room temperature
options.rationale: The compound contains ions, which students assume is enough on its own for conduction.

options.text: Sugar dissolved in water to make a solution
options.rationale: The rule 'dissolved conducts' is remembered without the condition that the particles must be charged.

options.text: Molten sugar, which melts to form a liquid
options.rationale: The rule 'melted conducts' is applied to a molecular substance, whose molecules carry no charge.

options.text: Sodium chloride solution in a beaker of water
options.rationale: Dissolving the ionic compound frees its ions to move, so charge can flow.

mcqs.stem: Which statement is true of substances that consist of small molecules?

options.text: They are always gases, whatever the conditions are
options.rationale: The first examples met are all gases, so 'usually' is hardened into 'always'.

options.text: They are usually gases or liquids at room temperature
options.rationale: The specification states that they are usually gases or liquids with relatively low melting and boiling points.

options.text: They are solids, because covalent bonds are strong
options.rationale: The strength of the covalent bonds inside the molecules is used to predict the state of the substance.

options.text: They have high melting points but low boiling points
options.rationale: The two temperatures are treated as independent, so one can be high while the other is low.

mcqs.stem: Liquid bromine, Br2, boils at 59 degrees C. What is overcome when it boils?

options.text: The weak intermolecular forces between Br2 molecules
options.rationale: It is the intermolecular forces, not the covalent bonds, that are overcome when a molecular substance boils.

options.text: The strong covalent bonds inside each Br2 molecule
options.rationale: Boiling is assumed to break the substance apart at its strongest bonds.

options.text: The electrostatic attraction between Br+ and Br- ions
options.rationale: Any strong attraction is assumed to be between oppositely charged ions, even between two non-metal atoms.

options.text: Both the covalent bonds and the forces between them
options.rationale: A hedged answer chosen by students unsure which of the two is actually overcome.

mcqs.stem: Substances made of small molecules melt at low temperatures even though their covalent bonds are strong. Why?

options.text: The covalent bonds inside molecules are actually weak
options.rationale: The low melting point is explained by assuming the covalent bonds must be weak after all.

options.text: The molecules are too light to hold each other in place
options.rationale: Mass is used in place of the strength of the forces between molecules.

options.text: The molecules push each other apart once they warm up
options.rationale: Melting is imagined as repulsion building up rather than as attraction being overcome.

options.text: Only the weak forces between molecules are overcome
options.rationale: Melting separates whole molecules, so only the weak intermolecular forces have to be overcome.

mcqs.stem: Substance A is made of small molecules and substance B is made of much larger molecules. Which statement is correct?

options.text: A has the higher boiling point, as its molecules pack in
options.rationale: Small molecules are pictured as sitting closer together and so being held more tightly.

options.text: B has the lower boiling point, as its molecules are slower
options.rationale: Mass and speed of movement replace the strength of the intermolecular forces.

options.text: B has the higher boiling point, as its forces are greater
options.rationale: Intermolecular forces increase with the size of the molecules, so larger molecules have higher boiling points.

options.text: A and B boil at the same temperature as one another
options.rationale: Molecular size is assumed to make no difference because both substances contain covalent bonds.

mcqs.stem: Why does methane, a substance made of small molecules, not conduct electricity?

options.text: Its covalent bonds hold all its electrons far too tightly
options.rationale: The metal explanation is carried over, so the answer looks for missing free electrons.

options.text: Its covalent bonds would have to break for charge to flow
options.rationale: Covalent bonds are brought in wherever an explanation about molecules is needed.

options.text: Its molecules have no overall electric charge to move
options.rationale: This is the specification's reason: the molecules do not have an overall electric charge.

options.text: Its molecules are far too large to move through a liquid
options.rationale: Conduction is assumed to require the molecules themselves to travel.

mcqs.stem: Water boils at 100 degrees C, but splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen needs a far greater energy input. Why?

options.text: Boiling breaks both O-H bonds; splitting rearranges atoms
options.rationale: Boiling is assumed to break covalent bonds, leaving only rearrangement for the harder process.

options.text: Boiling only separates molecules; splitting breaks bonds
options.rationale: Boiling overcomes weak intermolecular forces, while splitting must break strong covalent bonds inside the molecules.

options.text: The forces between water molecules are stronger than bonds
options.rationale: The comparison is reversed, because whatever holds the liquid together is assumed to be strongest.

options.text: Water is a liquid, so extra energy is required to split it
options.rationale: The state of the substance is offered in place of an explanation about bonding.

mcqs.stem: Why is poly(ethene) a solid at room temperature?

options.text: Its molecules are joined to each other by covalent bonds
options.rationale: Covalent bonding within the chains is extended to the links between separate chains.

options.text: Its covalent bonds are stronger than in small molecules
options.rationale: The strongest bonding in the structure is offered as the reason for the state.

options.text: Its very large molecules have strong forces between them
options.rationale: The intermolecular forces between polymer molecules are relatively strong, so polymers are solids at room temperature.

options.text: Its molecules are heavy enough to settle and stay still
options.rationale: Mass rather than force strength is used to explain why the substance is solid.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the bonding and forces in a polymer is correct?

options.text: Atoms within a chain are held by weak forces of attraction
options.rationale: The strong and weak labels are swapped between what is inside a molecule and what is between molecules.

options.text: Chains are joined to one another by strong covalent bonds
options.rationale: The covalent bonding along the chain is extended to the space between chains.

options.text: Chains are held to each other by attractions between ions
options.rationale: Any strong attraction is assumed to be electrostatic attraction between ions.

options.text: Atoms within a chain are joined by strong covalent bonds
options.rationale: The atoms in the polymer molecules are linked to other atoms by strong covalent bonds.

mcqs.stem: A diagram shows several long chains of repeating units lying side by side. What does the diagram show?

options.text: A giant covalent structure, such as diamond or silica
options.rationale: Both structures look large and covalently bonded, so the two diagrams are grouped together.

options.text: An ionic lattice, with the charges alternating regularly
options.rationale: A regular repeating pattern is taken as the signature of an ionic lattice.

options.text: A metal, with its layers of atoms stacked over each other
options.rationale: Chains lying side by side are read as the layers seen in diagrams of metals.

options.text: A polymer, whose chains are very large molecules
options.rationale: Separate long chains of repeating units are the recognisable feature of a polymer.

mcqs.stem: Why does silicon dioxide have a very high melting point?

options.text: Strong forces between its SiO2 molecules must be broken
options.rationale: Silicon dioxide is assumed to be molecular like carbon dioxide, so intermolecular forces are used.

options.text: Its silicon and oxygen ions attract in every direction
options.rationale: A high melting point is associated with ionic bonding, so ions are assumed to be present.

options.text: Its atoms are heavy, so a lot of heat energy is needed
options.rationale: Mass is used in place of the strength of the bonding.

options.text: Many strong covalent bonds must be overcome to melt it
options.rationale: In a giant covalent structure all the atoms are linked by strong covalent bonds, which must be overcome to melt it.

mcqs.stem: Which of these substances has a giant covalent structure?

options.text: Carbon dioxide, a gas made of small molecules
options.rationale: Carbon and covalent bonding are present, so it is assumed to be giant like diamond.

options.text: Sodium chloride, a compound of two elements
options.rationale: A giant regular lattice is recognised, but its ionic nature is missed.

options.text: Diamond, which is a form of the element carbon
options.rationale: The specification names diamond and graphite, forms of carbon, and silicon dioxide as giant covalent structures.

options.text: Copper, a metal used for electrical wiring
options.rationale: A giant structure is correctly identified, but it is a giant structure of atoms with metallic bonding.

mcqs.stem: A diagram shows a three-dimensional network in which every atom is joined on to others by strong bonds. What does it show?

options.text: A giant covalent structure, such as diamond
options.rationale: All the atoms being linked on to other atoms by strong covalent bonds identifies a giant covalent structure.

options.text: A giant ionic lattice, such as sodium chloride
options.rationale: Any three-dimensional lattice is assumed to be ionic, since that is where the word lattice was met.

options.text: A polymer, because all its chains are connected
options.rationale: Polymers and giant covalent structures are treated as the same kind of large covalent structure.

options.text: A metal, whose atoms sit in a regular pattern
options.rationale: Regularity is recognised, but metals are drawn as layers of identical atoms, not a bonded network.

mcqs.stem: Why do most metals have high melting points and boiling points?

options.text: They have giant structures with strong metallic bonding
options.rationale: Metals have giant structures of atoms with strong metallic bonding, so a great deal of energy is needed.

options.text: They have giant structures with weak metallic bonding
options.rationale: The structure is described correctly but the strength of the bonding is reversed.

options.text: Their atoms are heavy, needing much energy to be moved
options.rationale: Metals feel heavy, so mass is offered instead of the strength of the bonding.

options.text: Strong forces act between the separate metal molecules
options.rationale: Metals are assumed to be made of molecules, as other solids are believed to be.

mcqs.stem: Why can a pure metal be bent and shaped?

options.text: Its metallic bonds break easily when it is bent
options.rationale: Any change of shape is assumed to require something to break.

options.text: Its metal ions move out of the way when pushed
options.rationale: The ions are believed to be free to travel, as they are in a molten ionic compound.

options.text: Its atoms are round, so they roll over each other
options.rationale: The spheres in particle diagrams suggest rolling rather than layers sliding.

options.text: Its atoms are arranged in layers that can slide
options.rationale: In pure metals the atoms are arranged in layers, and it is the sliding of these layers that allows bending and shaping.

mcqs.stem: Why are alloys used instead of pure metals for many everyday objects?

options.text: Alloys are softer, so they can be shaped far more easily
options.rationale: Mixing is read as contamination that weakens the structure.

options.text: Alloys are pure substances, so they behave more reliably
options.rationale: Purity is associated with quality, and an alloy is assumed to be the purer material.

options.text: Alloys conduct electricity better than any pure metal does
options.rationale: A different useful metallic property is offered in place of hardness.

options.text: Alloys are harder than the pure metals they are made from
options.rationale: Pure metals are too soft for many uses, so they are mixed with other metals to make alloys, which are harder.

mcqs.stem: Why is copper a good conductor of electricity?

options.text: Delocalised electrons carry charge through the metal
options.rationale: This is the specification's reason: the delocalised electrons in the metal carry electrical charge through it.

options.text: Its positive metal ions move through the structure
options.rationale: The explanation for molten ionic compounds is transferred to metals, which also contain positive ions.

options.text: Its atoms pass electrons on from one to the next
options.rationale: A relay image replaces delocalisation, which is exactly what students find hard to picture.

options.text: Its layers of atoms slide, taking the charge along
options.rationale: The explanation for bending a metal is reused to explain conduction.

mcqs.stem: Why do metals conduct thermal energy well?

options.text: Energy is transferred by the delocalised electrons
options.rationale: The specification states that metals conduct thermal energy because energy is transferred by the delocalised electrons.

options.text: The metal ions themselves travel through the metal
options.rationale: The moving particle is taken to be the ion rather than the delocalised electron.

options.text: Metals are dense, so heat passes straight through
options.rationale: Metals feel heavy and cold, so density is offered as the explanation.

options.text: The layers of atoms slide and carry energy along
options.rationale: The explanation for malleability is reused for thermal conduction.
